The palace of Federico da Montefeltro in the hill town of Urbino in the Marche. Federico was one of the most successful condottieri, captains for hire, of the Renaissance; he became lord of Urbino in 1444 and its duke in 1474. Work began around the middle of the 15th century under the Florentine Maso di Bartolomeo, taking in an older palace. From 1466 to 1472 the Dalmatian architect Luciano Laurana directed the building, and Francesco di Giorgio Martini also had a part; who designed what is still argued. Donato Bramante, born in Urbino, may have worked on its completion.

Laurana's arcaded courtyard has a light, even rhythm ahead of what Florence was building at the time. Federico, a humanist as well as a soldier, filled the palace with rooms for study and built a great library. His studiolo, a room 3.6 m by 3.35 m, is lined with wood inlay that tricks the eye into seeing half-open cupboards of books, instruments, armour and caged parrots, with portraits of famous writers above. Below it lie two small chapels side by side, one Christian and one a Temple of the Muses.

Baldassare Castiglione set The Book of the Courtier in the palace in 1507. Today it houses the Galleria Nazionale delle Marche, with Piero della Francesca's Flagellation, works by Raphael, who was born in Urbino, and the Ideal City panel, sometimes given to Laurana. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1998.
